common_name: Mrs. Cholmondeley Clematis (Vigorous Pale Lavender-Blue Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Mrs. Cholmondeley is an old, exceptionally vigorous large-flowered cultivar that tolerates either light pruning (Group 2) or being cut back hard as Group 3 if it outgrows its space.

directions: Raised in England before 1900 and still among the most widely recommended large-flowered clematis for beginners, Mrs. Cholmondeley bears abundant pale lavender-blue flowers 6 to 8 inches across with prominent golden-yellow stamens. It is unusually vigorous and disease-resistant, flowering profusely from late spring through summer with sporadic rebloom into fall, and shrugs off the light pruning mistakes that trouble fussier large-flowered hybrids. Its reliability and long bloom season have earned it a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit.

common_name: Lasurstern Clematis (Deep Blue-Purple Wavy-Petaled Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Lasurstern blooms on old wood in late spring so should only be lightly tidied after flowering (Group 2), with a light second flush on new growth possible in late summer.

directions: Bred in Germany by Goos & Koenemann and introduced around 1905, Lasurstern produces large, deep blue-purple flowers up to 7 inches across with gently wavy, overlapping tepals and contrasting cream-white stamens. The first flush appears in late spring on the previous year's growth, often followed by a lighter repeat bloom on new growth in late summer. Its rich color and classic wide-open form have kept it a mainstay of large-flowered clematis collections for over a century.

common_name: Miss Bateman Clematis (White Large-Flowered Clematis with Red-Purple Anthers)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Miss Bateman flowers on old wood in late spring, so prune only lightly right after the main flush (Group 2).

directions: A Victorian-era English introduction, Miss Bateman bears creamy-white flowers with a faint central green bar and striking deep red-purple anthers that stand out sharply against the pale tepals. The main flush comes in late spring to early summer on the previous season's growth, occasionally followed by a smaller repeat bloom later in the season. Its crisp white-and-red coloring and moderate, well-behaved habit make it a favorite for growing through a modest obelisk or over a low wall.

common_name: Bees Jubilee Clematis (Mauve-Pink Large-Flowered Clematis with Carmine Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Bees Jubilee flowers on old wood in early summer, so limit pruning to light tidying after bloom (Group 2), and site out of hot afternoon sun so the bar color does not bleach.

directions: Introduced in the 1950s by the Bees of Chester nursery, this large-flowered hybrid bears mauve-pink tepals with a bold, deep carmine-pink central bar, giving each flower a strong bicolor pattern. Flowers open in early summer on the previous year's growth, with a lighter repeat flush later on new wood. Because the vivid bar color fades in strong sun, Bees Jubilee is often sited where it gets some midday shade, a niche many taller large-flowered cultivars cannot fill as well.

common_name: Elsa Spath Clematis (Deep Blue-Purple Large-Flowered Clematis, syn. Xerxes)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Elsa Spath flowers on both old and new wood, so use light pruning (Group 2) to preserve the earliest flush while still encouraging a strong repeat bloom.

directions: Raised in Germany and introduced in 1891, Elsa Spath (also sold in North America as 'Xerxes') produces deep violet-blue flowers up to 7 inches across with red-tinted anthers, opening in late spring and continuing intermittently into early fall, one of the longest bloom seasons among large-flowered clematis. Its rich, saturated color and dependable rebloom have kept it in cultivation for well over a century, and it performs reliably in both cool and warm-summer climates.

common_name: Countess of Lovelace Clematis (Double Lavender-Blue Early-Season Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; prune lightly (Group 2) to preserve the double flowers that form on old wood, since flowers produced later on new growth will be single.

directions: An English cultivar dating to the 1870s, Countess of Lovelace opens fully double, rosette-like lavender-blue flowers in late spring on the previous year's growth; a later flush produced on new growth is single rather than double, giving the vine two distinct looks across the season. The lush double blooms make it a favorite for close-up viewing near a patio or entryway, though it needs a sheltered spot and careful pruning to protect the old wood that produces its signature doubles.

common_name: Duchess of Sutherland Clematis (Rich Carmine-Red Late-Season Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Duchess of Sutherland blooms on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Named for the English aristocratic Leveson-Gower family, Duchess of Sutherland bears richly colored carmine-red to raspberry-pink flowers with a darker central bar, opening from midsummer into early fall on the current season's growth. Because it flowers entirely on new wood, it can be pruned hard every late winter like a viticella, making it an easy, low-maintenance way to bring saturated red tones into the late-summer garden.

common_name: John Huxtable Clematis (Pure White Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; John Huxtable is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: A vigorous viticella selection named for the English nurseryman who raised it, John Huxtable produces an abundance of pure white, four-tepaled flowers with cream stamens from midsummer into early fall. Its clean white color and reliable, profuse flowering on new wood make it a workhorse for covering fences, arbors, or scrambling through spent early-summer shrubs, and its hard-pruned Group 3 regime removes any guesswork for gardeners new to clematis.

common_name: Ramona Clematis (Lavender-Blue Large-Flowered Heirloom Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Ramona flowers on both old and new wood, so light pruning (Group 2) preserves the earliest flush while still allowing a strong late-season repeat.

directions: One of the oldest clematis cultivars still commonly grown in American gardens, Ramona bears large, pale lavender-blue flowers with cream stamens on a notably vigorous, heat-tolerant vine. It blooms heavily in early summer on the previous year's growth and continues sporadically into fall on new growth, and its exceptional tolerance of heat and humidity compared to many British-bred large-flowered hybrids has made it a long-standing favorite across the American Midwest and South.

common_name: Jackmanii Superba Clematis (Larger Richer-Purple Sport of Jackmanii)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Jackmanii Superba flowers on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3).

directions: A selected sport of the classic 1862 cultivar Jackmanii, Jackmanii Superba bears larger flowers of a richer, more velvety violet-purple with broader, overlapping tepals than the original. It flowers with great abundance on the current season's growth from midsummer into early fall, and like its parent tolerates hard annual pruning, heat, and a wide range of soils, making it one of the toughest and most floriferous large-flowered clematis for a first-time trellis or mailbox planting.

common_name: Huldine Clematis (Pearly White Viticella Clematis with Mauve Reverse)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Huldine is an extremely vigorous viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and should be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3), given a large sturdy support.

directions: An extremely vigorous French viticella cultivar dating to the early 20th century, Huldine produces pearly white, overlapping tepals with a soft pale mauve bar on the reverse that shows through beautifully when the flowers are backlit by afternoon sun. Blooming prolifically from midsummer well into fall on a vine that can easily reach 12 to 15 feet in a season, it needs a large, sturdy support such as a pergola or mature shrub, and its late, long bloom season makes it valuable for extending the clematis display after most large-flowered hybrids have finished.

common_name: Minuet Clematis (Creamy White Viticella Clematis with Purple-Pink Veining)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Minuet is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: A compact, free-flowering viticella cultivar, Minuet bears creamy white, bell-shaped flowers that flare open at the tips, each tepal heavily veined and edged in purple-pink so the overall effect reads as a soft bicolor. It blooms in great profusion from midsummer into early fall on new growth, and its modest ultimate size compared to other viticellas makes it a good choice for a large container or a more restrained trellis planting.

common_name: Venosa Violacea Clematis (White Viticella Clematis Netted with Purple Veins)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Venosa Violacea is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: A striking French viticella selection introduced in the late 19th century, Venosa Violacea bears white tepals dramatically netted with fine purple-violet veining and edged in a deeper purple margin, giving each flower a stained-glass appearance quite unlike the solid colors of most clematis. Flowering heavily from midsummer into fall on new growth, it is a long-standing favorite for adding textural, patterned color high on a fence or through a supporting shrub.

common_name: Royal Velours Clematis (Deep Velvety Purple-Red Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Royal Velours is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: A French-raised viticella cultivar, Royal Velours produces small but abundant nodding flowers in an intensely saturated, velvety purple-red that reads almost black-red in certain light. Flowering from midsummer into early fall on new growth, its modest flower size and huge quantity of bloom make it especially effective grown up through a spent early-summer shrub or a rose, where its deep color contrasts well with lighter companions.

common_name: Little Nell Clematis (White Viticella Clematis Edged in Pale Pink)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Little Nell is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: A dainty, free-flowering viticella cultivar, Little Nell bears white flowers with a delicate, narrow pale pink edge along each tepal, giving a soft, watercolor-like effect. It flowers profusely from midsummer into fall on new growth, and its restrained overall size compared to more rampant viticellas makes it well suited to a smaller obelisk, a large container, or a spot where a less overwhelming vine is wanted.

common_name: Freda Clematis Montana (Cerise-Pink Spring Clematis with Bronze Foliage)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Freda is a spring-blooming Clematis montana selection that flowers on the previous year's growth and should be pruned only right after flowering, if at all.

directions: A compact-growing selection of Clematis montana raised in England, Freda produces a profusion of deep cerise-pink flowers with a contrasting darker central bar, set off by bronze-purple young foliage that matures to green. Like other montanas it flowers in a single overwhelming spring flush on old wood, and its comparatively restrained size makes it more suitable than many montana cultivars for a medium-sized fence or arbor rather than requiring a whole tree or wall to cover.

common_name: Tetrarose Clematis Montana (Large Rosy-Lilac Tetraploid Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Tetrarose is a vigorous spring-blooming Clematis montana selection that needs a very sturdy, large support and should be pruned only right after flowering.

directions: A tetraploid selection of Clematis montana var. rubens, Tetrarose bears notably large, rosy-lilac flowers with thicker substance than the typical montana, set against bronze-purple young foliage. Like other montanas it produces a single spectacular flush of spring bloom on the previous year's growth, and its extra vigor and larger flower size have made it one of the most widely planted montana cultivars for covering a large wall, pergola, or mature tree.

common_name: Helios Clematis Tangutica (Upward-Facing Golden-Yellow Lantern Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below soil level and roots shaded, then let the twining vine climb a fence, arbor, or large shrub in full sun; Helios flowers on new wood and can be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: A compact selection of Clematis tangutica, Helios bears bright golden-yellow, lantern-shaped flowers held more outward- and upward-facing than the nodding blooms typical of the species, followed by the fluffy silvery seed heads characteristic of the group. It flowers from summer into fall on new growth and tolerates poor soil once established, and its more restrained habit compared to species tangutica or 'Bill MacKenzie' suits a smaller support or large container.

common_name: Sir Trevor Lawrence Clematis (Scarlet-Crimson Tulip-Form Texas Clematis)

planting.note: Pruning group three; blooms on new growth, so cut the vine back hard to a foot or so above the ground each late winter.

directions: Named for a 19th-century president of the Royal Horticultural Society, this Texas-parentage hybrid produces nodding, tulip-shaped flowers in glowing scarlet-crimson with a paler, lighter interior, opening from midsummer into fall on a wiry, more restrained vine than the large-flowered hybrids. Like other texensis cultivars it tolerates heat and dry spells better than most clematis, and because it flowers entirely on new wood, the whole vine can be cut back hard each late winter to renew vigor and maximize bloom.

common_name: Blue Angel Clematis (Pale Sky-Blue Late-Season Clematis, syn. Blekitny Aniol)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Blue Angel flowers on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Bred in Poland by the noted clematis hybridizer Brother Stefan Franczak and sold internationally under the English translation of its name, Blue Angel bears pale, soft sky-blue nodding flowers with slightly twisted, pointed tepals. It flowers over an unusually long season from midsummer into early fall on the current year's growth, and its gentle pastel color and profuse bloom make it a popular pairing with roses and other summer-blooming shrubs.
